Part 1: Partial Derivatives¶

(a)¶

Compute the derivative $\partial L / \partial x(i).$ Leaving all other variables fixed, what value of $x(i)$ minimizes $L$?

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x(i)} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\partial |\mu - x(j)|}{\partial x(i)} + \frac{\partial (\lambda \mu^2)}{\partial x(i)} $$ let $ f(x) = |x| $ then $ f'(x) = sign(x)$ where $$ \operatorname{sign}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases} $$ so $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x(i)} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\partial f(\mu - x(j))}{\partial x(i)} + 0 $$ the only time when the partial derivative of x(i) is non-zero for the sum terms is when j=i so $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x(i)} = f'(\mu - x(i)) * (\mu - x(i))' $$ $$ = sign(\mu - x(i)) * (-1) $$ and therefore, $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x(i)} = -sign(\mu - x(i)) $$

When is L minimal?¶

For x(i) to minimize L, we need $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x(i)}$ to be equal to 0 or the derivative to change sign from before that point to after that point (from negative to positive)
When $ \mu = x(i) $ , $sign(\mu - x(i))$ is not defined but by drawing the function we can see that the derivative/slope before is negative and after is positive and that L (looks like a V) will be minimal there.

(b)¶

Compute the derivative $\partial L / \partial \mu.$ If $\lambda = 0,$ what values of $\mu$ minimize $L$?

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\partial |\mu - x(j)|}{\partial \mu} + \frac{\partial (\lambda \mu^2)}{\partial \mu} $$ let $ f(x) = |x| $ then $ f'(x) = sign(x)$ where $$ \operatorname{sign}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases} $$ so $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\partial f(\mu - x(j))}{\partial \mu} + 2\lambda\mu $$ $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} f'(\mu - x(j)) * (\mu - x(j))' + 2\lambda\mu $$ $$ = \sum_{j=1}^{N} sign(\mu - x(j)) * (1) + 2\lambda\mu $$ and therefore, $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} sign(\mu - x(j)) + 2\lambda\mu $$

If $\lambda = 0,$ what values of $\mu$ minimize $L$?¶

If $\lambda = 0$, the second term of $\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu}$ is also 0 so the only significant term left is the sum.
To minimize a function, we want to find when the derivative is equal to 0
The question becomes, what values of $\mu$ makes $\sum_{j=1}^{N} sign(\mu - x(j))$ as close to 0 as possible
The sum will be closest to 0 when $\mu$ has as many x(j) on the left and on the right
This means that the first terms of the sum will be 1 and the last will be -1. Ideally we have as many -1s as 1s and then the sum will be exactly 0
There are two cases:
There is an odd amount of x(i): $\mu$ should just be the middle value of the set of x(j)
There is an even amount of x(i): $\mu$ can be any value between the two middle values of the set x(j)

(c)¶

Compute the derivative $\partial L / \partial \theta.$

With the chain rule, we can rewrite the problem: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu}.\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial \theta} $$

We know from exercise b) that: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} sign(\mu - x(j)) + 2\lambda\mu $$

and $ \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial \theta} = 3\theta^2 $ since $\mu = \theta^3 $

Therefore,

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = (\sum_{j=1}^{N} sign(\theta^3 - x(j)) + 2\lambda\theta^3) . 3\theta^2 $$

(d)¶

Compute $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \operatorname{softmax}(z)_j. $$ (Hint: first define $Z = \ln \sum_{l = 1}^k e^{z_l}$ and compute $\partial Z / \partial z_j.$)

We know the chain rule for ln gives us this: $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \ln \operatorname{f}(x) = \frac{1}{\operatorname{f}(x)} . \operatorname{f'}(x) $$

First I define $Z = \ln \sum_{l = 1}^k e^{z_l}$
Then $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} Z = \frac{1}{\sum_{l=1}^k e^{z_l}} . \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \sum_{l=1}^k e^{z_l} $$ The second term can be reduced to only $ e^{z_i} $ since all the other terms of the sum are constants
Therefore, we get $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} Z = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{l=1}^k e^{z_l}} $$ This is exactly our $\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i$ so $ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} Z = \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i $

Now, we go back to our original function that we want to compute: $ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \operatorname{softmax}(z)_j$ Using the ln rules we can rewrite this as $$ = \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{l=1}^k e^{z_l}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln e^{z_j} - \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \sum_{l=1}^k e^{z_l} $$ The second term is exactly $\frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} Z $ which we already have. We replace it: $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \operatorname{softmax}(z)_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln e^{z_j} - \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i $$

Now we compute: $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln e^{z_j} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} z_j $$ There are two cases, either j = i and then the result is 1. Otherwise it's 0.
Let $$ \operatorname{is_i}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x = i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise } \end{cases} $$ Then $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln e^{z_j} = \operatorname{is_i}(j) $$
When we put everything together: $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \operatorname{softmax}(z)_j = \operatorname{is_i}(j) - \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i $$

Part 2: Linear Regression¶

(a)¶

Consider the linear model, defined by parameters $(\theta_0, \theta_1)$, which predicts $$ \hat y(i) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) $$ for each index $i.$ Express the gradient $\nabla L$ of mean squared error as a function of the parameter vector $\theta$ and the datapoints $(x(i), y(i)).$

The mean squared error is: $$L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) - y(i))^2$$ First, the partial derivative w.r.t. $\theta_0$: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_0} = \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) - y(i))$$ Next, the partial derivative w.r.t. $\theta_1$: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_1} = \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) - y(i))\,x(i)$$ The gradient is: $$\nabla L = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) - y(i)) \\ \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\theta_0 + \theta_1 x(i) - y(i))\,x(i) \end{bmatrix}$$

Part 3: k-Means and PCA¶

(a)¶

Suppose we didn't have access to the species attribute of the iris dataset. Implement the Lloyd-Forgy algorithm for $k$-means and use it to infer a partition of the iris dataset into three species. Compute the confusion matrix and the accuracy of the partition relative to the true species.

In [6]:
iris = iml.load_iris()

X = iris.data
y_true = iris.target

print("Data shape:", X.shape)
print("Number of species:", len(iris.target_names))
print("Species:", iris.target_names)

Data shape: (150, 4)
Number of species: 3
Species: ['setosa' 'versicolor' 'virginica']
In [7]:
def k_means(X, k, max_iterations=100):
    # choose initial centroids randomly
    random_indices = np.random.choice(len(X), size=k, replace=False)
    centroids = X[random_indices].copy()
    for i in range(max_iterations):

        distances = np.linalg.norm(X[:, np.newaxis] - centroids, axis=2)  # calculate distances

        labels = np.argmin(distances, axis=1)  # assign points to clusters

        # recalculate centroids
        new_centroids = np.array([
            X[labels == c].mean(axis=0) if np.any(labels == c) else centroids[c]
            for c in range(k)
        ])
        # if centroids stop changing -> stop
        if np.allclose(centroids, new_centroids):
            break

        centroids = new_centroids

    return labels, centroids

In [9]:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
from itertools import permutations

best_accuracy = 0

for permutation in permutations(range(3)):
    y_pred_mapped = np.array([permutation[label] for label in y_pred])
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred_mapped)

    if accuracy > best_accuracy:
        best_accuracy = accuracy
        best_prediction = y_pred_mapped

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, best_prediction)

print("Confusion matrix:")
print(cm)

print("Accuracy:", best_accuracy)
print("Accuracy (%):", best_accuracy * 100)

Confusion matrix:
[[50  0  0]
 [ 0 48  2]
 [ 0 14 36]]
Accuracy: 0.8933333333333333
Accuracy (%): 89.33333333333333

We implemented the Lloyd-Forgy k-means algorithm using Numpy. We initialized three random centroids and assigned each observation to its nearest centroid using Euclidean distance.
Then recalculated the centroids as the mean of the observations in each cluster. This process was repeated until the centroids stopped changing.

Since k-means assigns arbitrary numbers to clusters, we matched the predicted cluster labels with the actual species labels before calculating the confusion matrix and accuracy.

The reported accuracy was 89.33%. Setosa was perfectly separated, while some of the versicolor and virginica observations were assigned to the wrong cluster. This shows that these two species are more difficult to distinguish using k-means.

DBSCAN cluster sizes:
0    1808
1    6935
2      35
Name: count, dtype: int64

The projection onto the first two columns shows a parallelogram point cloud with the letters "uni.lu" visible. This suggests the data were generated by placing points in a rectangular region and removing points in the shape of the letters. This is an inference from the plot because the plot alone does not establish the exact generation process.

We standardized the three columns and applied PCA. The first two principal components explain about 97.29% of the variance, so the 2D PCA plot preserves most of the variation in the data. Its rotation relative to the column projection is expected, because PCA uses new axes.

K-means (k=3) divides the point cloud into three broad regions that cut across the letter pattern. DBSCAN is density-based: the cluster with 1808 points is the letters "uni.lu", the cluster with 6935 points is the background, and the 35-point cluster is the dot of the "i". It recovers the letters, while K-means cuts across them, so we consider DBSCAN the more reasonable method here.
